youtube_title: Ireland's Supreme Court Said Subway's Bread Isn't Bread (for Tax) 🦝⚖️
caption: In Bookfinders v Revenue Commissioners (2020), Ireland's Supreme Court held the Subway bread at issue exceeded the VAT law's 2% sugar limit for 'bread', so it didn't qualify for the zero rate.
script: Ireland's Supreme Court ruled that Subway's bread isn't legally bread, at least for tax. [disclaimer] Here's the background. In Ireland, bread can qualify for a zero rate of VAT. But the tax law defines bread narrowly. Ingredients like sugar and fat can't be more than two percent of the weight of the flour. A Subway franchisee, a company called Bookfinders, wanted VAT refunds from two thousand four and two thousand five, on bread, hot sandwiches, tea and coffee. The tax office said no. The company lost at every level: the appeal commissioner, the High Court, the Court of Appeal, and finally the Supreme Court, in September twenty twenty. The key fact? Subway's recipe called for sugar at about ten percent of the flour's weight. That's five times the limit. And the court said that if even one ingredient goes over its limit, the product falls outside the legal definition of bread. It added that tax exemptions are read strictly. The argument about the hot sandwiches failed too, because it depended on the bread qualifying. So the headlines said Subway bread isn't bread. More precisely, this recipe didn't fit Ireland's VAT definition of bread. The court didn't ban the bread, and it wasn't ruling on baking. [loop] So the next time you order a sandwich in Ireland, remember
